slides.title:
Build a research loop.
Then give it an agent.
slides.body:
A four-hour experiment in the Solar Forecasting Lab.
Solar forecasting, experiment tracking, and agents that edit research code.
slides.notes: We’ll build two small forecasts from real solar observations. First we’ll write and track the experiments ourselves. Then we’ll let a research agent propose changes to the image model’s code. The pixel lab is an illustration; the observations and recorded results come from the workshop dataset.

slides.title: Your team has a promising result.
slides.body:
“The new model looks better.”THE RESEARCH UPDATE · FICTIONAL SCENE

You ask which run.

Someone shares a screenshot.

You ask which code.

Someone shares a notebook called final.

There are four notebooks called final.
slides.notes: Imagine a teammate says the new model is better, but can only find a screenshot and several notebooks called final. That’s our fictional opening. Ask the room what they would need before trusting or repeating the comparison.

slides.title: Two forecasts from real solar observations
slides.body:
Real training observations. NOAA GOES-15 and NASA/SDO AIA 171 Å; prepared with SunPy.

Measurements: use the previous hour to predict flux 30 minutes ahead.

Images: use two observations to predict an image one hour ahead.
slides.notes: Read the instruments before discussing models. The left plot measures solar X-ray flux; the right image records extreme-ultraviolet light at 171 Å. These are real February 2014 observations, prepared at a small scale for CPU teaching. The image uses false color. We are testing forecasts, not predicting a reliable flare warning.

slides.title: First reproduce a result. Then try to improve it.
slides.body:
“Could an agent try the next experiment?”THE LAB’S NEXT REQUEST

First, you build the experiment.

Define the target, train a model, and save what ran.

Then the agent changes its code.

Review the change, run it, and compare the prediction.
slides.notes: The reason for building the experiment stack comes first: we need to know whether a change helped and be able to repeat it. Once that works, the same loop can test code proposed by an agent. The language model stays fixed. The small forecasting model trains normally.

slides.title: Build a forecast, then test changes to its code
slides.body:
Forecast

Load observations and write a baseline.

Track

Save code, settings, weights, and predictions.

Improve

Review and test the agent’s code changes.

Evaluate

Compare the selected models on later dates.

You’ll edit Python in your own notebook and publish the results to your project.
slides.notes: Follow this sequence in the notebook. You’ll change Python, run a check, execute the experiment, and open the resulting evidence in Forge. A change that fails to improve the forecast is still something we can investigate.

slides.title: Predict X-ray flux 30 minutes ahead
slides.body: Predict log10 XRS-B flux. A forecast window includes observations, timestamps, and a future target.
slides.notes: Read the timeline from left to right. The model gets sixty minutes of observed flux, then predicts the reading thirty minutes after now. We work in log10 flux, so the error is in transformed units rather than raw watts per square metre.

slides.title: Use earlier dates to train, later dates to test
slides.body: February 2014, UTC. Fit normalization on training data only.
slides.notes: Train on February 1–10, choose models using February 11–12, and leave February 13–14 for the final comparison. Every input and the target of a window must belong to one partition. Fit normalization using training data only.

slides.title: Leave out windows with missing observations
slides.body:
Check the timestamps

The prepared GOES archive has no data for February 8.

A window needs its full input history and its future target.

Skip an incomplete window

Keep the missing date in the coverage record.

A zero would invent a measurement that the instrument never supplied.

Use the same accepted windows for every model in the comparison.
slides.notes: February 8 is absent from the prepared GOES source archive. A window that needs those readings cannot be used. Filling the absence with zero would tell the model that the instrument measured zero flux, which it did not.

slides.title: Start by copying the latest reading
slides.body:
```python def persistence_forecast(split): # Latest observed value becomes the future prediction. ... ```

Predict flux 30 minutes ahead by copying the latest reading.

This uses only a reading we already have. It does not look at the future target.
Input: The latest observed reading in each windowOutput: One 30-minute-ahead prediction per window
slides.notes: Persistence means predicting that the latest value will stay the same. Solar observations are correlated over time, so this simple baseline can be hard to beat. It gives us a comparison before we spend time training a network.

slides.title: Measure how far the prediction missed
slides.body:
```python error = mean(abs(predicted_log_flux - observed_log_flux)) ```

Lower is better

The same target, transform, and units apply to every run.

Look at individual misses

Inspect the times where the forecast misses.

Compare each prediction with the observed future, then average the errors.
Input: Predictions and matching future observationsOutput: One mean absolute error in log-flux units
slides.notes: For each forecast, subtract the observed log-flux target, take the absolute error, then average across windows. Lower is better. The average can hide a bad interval, so we also inspect the curves. Keep flux error separate from the later image score.

slides.notes: Allow ten minutes. Let participants attempt the function before opening the answer. Ask them to find an interval where the real flux changed while persistence kept the previous value. That is a concrete error another model could try to reduce.

slides.title: Predict the solar image one hour ahead
slides.body: AIA 171 Å. Prepared 64 × 64 arrays. One-hour forecasting.
slides.notes: Now we give the model images from sixty minutes ago and now, and ask for the image sixty minutes ahead. The AIA 171 Å arrays are 64 by 64 pixels so the exercise can run on CPU.

slides.title: Save image experiments the same way
slides.body: The input and prediction changed shape. Source, settings, weights, and evidence still belong together. The image score uses normalized log1p intensity.
slides.notes: The inputs are now images, but we still save the same kinds of records: data, code, settings, weights, and predictions. Image values use normalized log1p intensity, so their errors have a different scale from the GOES errors.

slides.title: See exactly which images become input and target
slides.body:
First accepted training window. All three images share the same intensity scale.
The target is hidden from the model during prediction. It is used afterward to measure the miss.
slides.notes: Read the observation times. Channel zero is the earlier image; channel one is the current image. The third image is the future target. These are three real observations from a training window, not three outputs of an AI image generator.

slides.title: Two image channels enter. One forecast comes out.
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="residual" :reveal="1" />
slides.notes: Here the network predicts the entire future image. A batch has two input channels, each 64 by 64. The output has one channel. The forward function returns self.net(x). Keep this geometry in view for the residual reveal.

slides.title: Let the current image carry what has not changed
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="residual" :reveal="2" />
slides.notes: The network now predicts a correction. The arrow around the network copies the current input image and adds the correction to it. In x[:, 1:2], the slice keeps the channel dimension, giving batch by one by 64 by 64. Zero correction returns persistence exactly. That is the behavior participants add to forward.

slides.title: Write the addition you just traced
slides.body:
```python def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) # [batch, 1, 64, 64] current_image = x[:, 1:2] # keep the channel axis return current_image + correction ```
Input: earlier image + current imageOutput: one future image per example

Check: if correction is zero, the forecast equals the current image.
slides.notes: The diagram and code describe the same addition. Ask participants why x[:, 1] would remove a dimension and why x[:, 1:2] preserves it. The notebook implementation also branches on architecture so the convolutional comparison still returns only the network output.

slides.title: Count errors on the solar disk
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="mask" />
slides.notes: This is a diagram of the scoring calculation, not a forecast. The fixed mask assigns one to disk pixels and zero outside. Multiply absolute errors by the mask, average over the selected pixels per image, then average images. A changed off-disk pixel must not affect the score.

slides.title: Write the scorer, then test a deliberate miss
slides.body:
```python absolute_error = np.abs(prediction - target) per_image = (absolute_error * disk_mask).sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```
Identical arrays: score 0Every disk pixel +1: score 1Only off-disk pixels +1: score 0
slides.notes: Run the three local examples before training. They explain what the scorer measures. The participant writes this development scorer, and the protected primary scorer checks the comparison with the same published rule. Missing or invalid predictions are not zero error.

slides.title: Train with one loss; compare with a fixed metric
slides.body:
Training lossPrimary evaluation metric
Supplies gradients while fitting weightsMeasures predictions for comparison
Candidate code can change itFixed outside candidate code
The starting implementation uses squared errorThe image comparison uses masked absolute error
slides.notes: The training loss supplies gradients that update weights. The evaluation metric tells us how the forecast compares with another model. We can try a different training loss while keeping the scoring rule fixed. That will be one of the agent’s recorded proposals.

slides.title: Ask for two changes to the same starting code
slides.body: Harness²-inspired: our probes train forecasting weights and include validation scores.
slides.notes: Both candidates start from the same code and settings. This borrows Propose–Probe–Compose from Harness². Here the probes train forecasting models and give validation scores to the editor, so it is a teaching adaptation rather than the paper’s exact task protocol.

slides.title: The first proposal changes one loss operation
slides.body:
```python def training_loss(prediction, target, mask): # Before: square each miss. # After: take its absolute size. return ((prediction - target).abs() * mask).sum() / mask.sum() ```
− (prediction - target).square()
+ (prediction - target).abs()

Agent’s hypothesis: training on absolute error may help the fixed absolute-error score. The probe tests that claim.
slides.notes: This is the actual first-round Candidate A edit in v0.3.0. It changes the training objective, while the evaluation scorer remains fixed. The alternative candidate retains the original squared loss. The diff establishes the proposed change; it does not establish an improvement until both run.

slides.title: Train and score each candidate
slides.body: Use the same training and validation data. Keep failed runs visible.
slides.notes: Train each candidate on the same training dates and compare its validation error. If one fails before producing a forecast, inspect the error and leave its score missing.

slides.title: Ask the agent which changes to keep
slides.body: The agent can keep A, keep B, combine changes, or retain the starting code.
slides.notes: The agent reads both test results and can keep one candidate, combine changes, or retain the starting code. The dashed lines mean that it reviewed the results. They do not mean both sets of changes were merged.

slides.title: Test the version the agent chose
slides.body: Run the selected code on the same training and validation dates.
slides.notes: Run the chosen code before accepting it. Combining two changes can behave differently from either one alone. If the unchanged version is retained, testing it creates another execution of the same code.

slides.title: Open the training call behind the chosen version
slides.body:

slides.title: Put the attribute inside the tool scope
slides.body:
```python
def instrument_tool(observation):
    with tracing.Tool(
        name=observation["name"],
        arguments=observation["arguments"],
        result=observation["result"],
        started_at=stamp(observation["started_at"]),
        ended_at=stamp(observation["ended_at"]),
    ) as tool:
        tool.set_attributes({"workshop.exercise": "solar-research"})
        if observation.get("error"):
            tool.record_error(RuntimeError(observation["error"]))
```
slides.notes: The attribute is attached inside the Tool scope. The complete notebook function also supplies its call identity and outer conversation. Use the operation’s timestamps so Agent Lens shows when the work happened, not when it was uploaded.

slides.title: Return a copy of the latest observation
slides.notes: The prepared split includes the last observed reading for each forecast window. Return a copy so later changes to the prediction array cannot alter the dataset.

slides.title: Take the mean of the absolute errors
slides.notes: Subtract prediction and target, take absolute values, and average. A prediction of one against a target of zero gives one. These are log10 flux units. The training loss above it is separate and uses squared error.

slides.title: Compare the settings and loss curves
slides.body:
Open two runs from the Sweep. Compare their model, width, learning rate, and training steps.

Then open the loss curves. A lower validation error is easier to interpret when you can see how each model trained.

If a run failed, inspect its error. A missing score cannot rank that model.
slides.notes: Open the configuration and curve for two runs. Find the settings they share and the value that differs. If training failed, inspect the error rather than assigning a score to a forecast that does not exist.

slides.title: Average the error inside the disk mask
slides.body:
```python def my_image_mae(prediction, target, disk_mask): errors = np.abs(prediction - target) * disk_mask per_image = errors.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```

Test zero error, constant +1 error, and an error only outside the mask.
slides.notes: The mask selects the solar disk. Compute the sum and count per image, then average across images. Check identical arrays, a constant one-unit difference, and a difference only outside the mask.

slides.title: Add the correction to input channel 1
slides.body:
```python def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) if architecture == "residual": return x[:, 1:2] + correction return correction ```
The current image is input channel 1. The return has one channel.
slides.notes: Channel zero is the earlier image and channel one is the current image. Add the correction to channel one. With a zero correction, this function returns the current image exactly.

slides.title: Round 2: start the correction at zero
slides.body:
```python if architecture == 'residual': nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].weight) nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].bias) # The residual forward pass remains: return prediction + x[:, 1:2] ```
The round-one absolute loss stays. Zero initial correction makes the initial forecast persistence.
